title: Cell division by meiosis and sexual reproduction

beats.say: Open like a teacher: the number puzzle. Body cells have 46 chromosomes; a baby gets half from each parent; so what must the sex cells have? Curious. No questions.

lines.text: body cells:  46 chromosomes.     egg + sperm  →  baby with 46
lines.say: Here's a puzzle. Every human body cell has forty-six chromosomes. A baby starts when an egg joins a sperm. And the baby needs forty-six too. So how many chromosomes must the egg and the sperm each have? We worked out last time that it can't be forty-six. Today's answer is meiosis.

beats.say: Diploid (2n, in pairs) and haploid (n, single set). Humans: 23 pairs; gametes 23. Gametes are sex cells. No questions.

lines.text: {{diploid|ul.p}} (2n):  chromosomes in PAIRS.   Humans:  23 pairs, 46 chromosomes
lines.say: Body cells have their chromosomes in pairs, one of each pair from each parent. We call that diploid. In humans that's twenty-three pairs, forty-six chromosomes.

lines.text: {{haploid|ul.b}} (n):  a SINGLE set.   Human gametes:  23 chromosomes
lines.say: A haploid cell has just one chromosome from each pair: a single set. Human sex cells have twenty-three chromosomes.

lines.text: gametes = sex cells:  sperm and egg (animals),  pollen grain and ovule (flowering plants)
lines.say: The sex cells are called gametes: sperm and egg in animals, pollen grains and ovules in flowering plants.

beats.say: Meiosis: a reduction division. One diploid cell makes four haploid cells, genetically different. Each gamete gets one chromosome from every pair. No questions.

lines.text: {{Meiosis|ul.p}}: a {{reduction division|ul}}.   1 diploid cell  →  4 haploid cells
lines.say: Meiosis is a reduction division. One diploid cell divides to make four haploid cells, each with half the chromosomes.

lines.text: each gamete gets ONE chromosome from EVERY pair
lines.say: And each gamete doesn't get any random chromosomes. It gets exactly one from every pair, so it has a complete single set.

lines.text: the 4 cells are genetically DIFFERENT from each other
lines.say: And the four cells aren't identical to each other. The way the pairs separate is shuffled differently each time, so each gamete gets a different mix.

beats.say: Fertilisation restores the number: haploid sperm fuses with haploid egg to give a diploid zygote, 23 plus 23 gives 46. The zygote then divides by mitosis to form the embryo. No questions.

lines.text: sperm nucleus:  23 chromosomes        egg nucleus:  23 chromosomes
lines.say: So here are the numbers. The sperm nucleus has twenty-three chromosomes, and so does the egg nucleus.

lines.text: {{Fertilisation|ul.p}}:  the two nuclei fuse  →  a {{zygote|ul}} with 46 chromosomes, 23 pairs
lines.say: At fertilisation the two nuclei fuse together, giving a cell called a zygote, with twenty-three plus twenty-three, forty-six chromosomes, back in pairs. Diploid again.

lines.text: the zygote divides by MITOSIS  →  embryo
lines.say: Then the zygote divides by mitosis, not meiosis, to grow into an embryo, keeping forty-six in every cell.

beats.say: A friend says the zygote keeps dividing by meiosis to make the embryo. Test with numbers: 46 would halve to 23, then 11.5 which is impossible. Detective tone, no questions.

board.text: A friend's idea: embryo by meiosis

lines.text: zygote:  46 chromosomes
lines.say: A friend of mine says the embryo is made by the zygote dividing by meiosis. Let's test it with numbers. The zygote has forty-six chromosomes.

lines.text: by meiosis:  46 → 23 → 11.5 ??
lines.say: If it divided by meiosis, the cells would have twenty-three, and the next division would give eleven and a half. You can't have half a chromosome.

lines.text: Mitosis copies every chromosome  →  every cell keeps 46
lines.say: Mitosis copies the chromosomes first, so every cell of the embryo keeps forty-six. Embryos grow by mitosis; only gametes are made by meiosis.

beats.say: A friend says gametes get any 23 random chromosomes, and that all sperm from one man are identical. Test both. Detective tone, no questions.

lines.text: any 23 chromosomes at random?
lines.say: Two more ideas. First: a gamete gets any twenty-three chromosomes at random.

lines.text: Then a gamete might get 2 copies of one pair and none of another
lines.say: Test: if it were random, a gamete could end up with two of one pair, and none of another. The baby would be missing instructions.

lines.text: Meiosis gives exactly ONE from each of the 23 pairs
lines.say: What really happens is that meiosis gives exactly one from each of the twenty-three pairs, so nothing is missing.

lines.text: all sperm from one man identical?
lines.say: Second idea: all the sperm from one man are identical.

lines.text: Each pair separates independently  →  many different combinations
lines.say: But each pair separates independently of the others, so each sperm gets a different combination. So they are all different.

beats.say: Variation: meiosis shuffles chromosomes and random fertilisation combines gametes in different ways, so offspring differ. Variation is the raw material for natural selection. No questions.

lines.text: meiosis shuffles chromosomes   →   different gametes
lines.say: Two things create variation. First, meiosis shuffles the chromosomes, so every gamete is different.

lines.text: random fertilisation   →   any egg can meet any sperm
lines.say: Second, fertilisation is random. Any sperm can meet any egg, in different combinations.

lines.text: So brothers and sisters from the same parents are genetically different
lines.say: That's why brothers and sisters look different, even with the same parents.

lines.text: variation is the raw material for natural selection
lines.say: This variation is important, because it is the raw material for natural selection.
